item.title: Why You Hear What You Expect to Hear
item.description:
Cognition

Why You Hear What You Expect to Hear

When the brain fills in the blanks.

Posted June 12, 2026

Key points
  • Science shows that speech perception is not objective, it is constructive.
  • Hearing errors reveal that we don’t simply hear speech, we also interpret it.
  • We often mishear words because the brain doesn’t just listen, it actively predicts what it expects to hear.
Source: beast01/Shutterstock

“‘Scuse me while I kiss this guy.”

For decades, listeners have confidently misheard this lyric from Jimi Hendrix’s Purple Haze, despite the actual line being “’Scuse me while I kiss the sky.” Misheard phrases like this are often called mondegreens, a term coined by writer Sylvia Wright in 1954 after she misheard a line in a Scottish ballad.

Speech Is Messy

Mondegreens are often humorous, but they highlight something fundamental about language: we don’t simply hear speech, we also interpret it.

Interpretation, as it turns out, is deeply shaped by expectation. In everyday conversation, speech is not neatly separated into individual words. Sounds overlap, blend, and influence one another in a continuous stream known as connected speech. Add background noise, accents, and rapid delivery, and the signal reaching the ear is often incomplete or ambiguous.

Yet we rarely notice this difficulty. We usually understand speech with remarkable speed and accuracy. This is because the brain is not waiting passively for perfect input. It actively reconstructs meaning from partial information. (Stollznow, 2026)

What Is the Ganong Effect?

One of the clearest demonstrations of this reconstructive process is the Ganong effect, first described by psychologist William Ganong. (Ganong, 1980)

In experiments, participants hear speech sounds that fall between two sounds. For example, something ambiguous between a “g” and a “k” sound. Crucially, the sound is placed in different word contexts. When the ambiguous sound precedes “-ift,” listeners tend to hear gift rather than the non-word kift. But when the same sound precedes “-iss,” they tend to hear kiss rather than giss.

In short, people are biased toward hearing real words. The brain is not just decoding sound, it’s choosing the most plausible word match.

The Ganong effect demonstrates that speech perception is not purely bottom-up (that is, data-driven). It is also top-down (i.e., our knowledge base). Bottom-up processing refers to the raw sensory input arriving from the ears. For example, hearing a word in a noisy room or a sound like a dog barking that is partially masked by other noise. Top-down processing refers to the influence of knowledge, expectations, and context. In real-world listening, these systems work together. But when speech is ambiguous, top-down knowledge often takes control, steering perception toward familiar, meaningful words.

Why the Brain “Fixes” What It Hears

This bias toward real words is not a flaw in perception. It is a feature of an efficient system. It’s also what underpins effects like the “telephone game,” where a message becomes progressively reshaped as it is passed from person to person, with each listener unconsciously imposing form, meaning, or familiar word patterns onto ambiguous input.

In everyday environments, speech is rarely pristine. The brain prioritizes meaning over acoustic precision, quickly resolving uncertainty by drawing on stored vocabulary and context. This is why we can understand a friend speaking in a noisy café or follow dialogue in a poorly recorded phone call. The brain is constantly filling in the gaps.

When the Brain Fills in the Blanks

This same mechanism also explains why we sometimes mishear speech in very specific ways. The Ganong effect is closely related to another phenomenon known as phonemic restoration. (Munechika, et al., 2026) In these cases, listeners perceive missing sounds as present when they are replaced by noise, such as a cough or static.

Even when part of a word is physically absent, the brain restores it if the context strongly supports a meaningful interpretation. In both cases, perception is shaped as much by what we expect as by what is actually there.

The Ganong effect shows that speech perception is not a passive recording of sound, but an active process of interpretation. We do not simply hear language, we negotiate it. The brain constantly balances sensory input with linguistic knowledge, resolving ambiguity in real time.

Most of the time, this system works beautifully. Occasionally, it produces humor, like mondegreens. At other times, it reveals that perception is not objective, it is constructive.

We don’t always hear what is said. We hear what we expect to hear.

item.title: Food as Treatment for PTSD
item.description:
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder

Food as Treatment for PTSD

Learn what to eat and what not to eat for PTSD treatment.

Posted June 12, 2026

Key points
  • A helpful adjunctive treatment for PTSD is a targeted diet.
  • Foods to avoid for PTSD: sugar, fast food, fried foods, and high-GI carbs like white bread.
  • Blueberries, Omega-3s, and Vitamin E are linked to decreased PTSD symptoms.

Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a mental health disorder that develops after experiencing or witnessing a traumatic event, for example, war, a serious accident, or abuse. Treatment usually includes medication, psychotherapy, and adjunctive treatments such as aerobic exercise, yoga, getting proper sleep, utilizing stress management techniques, and choosing food wisely.

What we eat has a major influence on how our brains function. This is partly because of the strong link between the brain and our GI tract. The vagus nerve runs from the brainstem to the GI tract and interacts with the nerves embedded in the gut wall. There is two-way communication between the brain and the gut. Each one influences the other.

Also, the gut has a microbiome consisting of millions of bacteria, fungi, and viruses. It plays a major role in digestion, the functions of the immune system, and produces neurotransmitters such as serotonin, dopamine, and GABA. Furthermore, the gut microbiome is involved in the permeability of the blood-brain barrier, brain volume, neurocircuitry, and other brain functions (MacKay, 2024).

The microbiome is powerfully influenced by what we eat. Food provides nutrients for the microbes, helps determine which species will predominate, and what metabolic products are made by them. Given the tight connection between the brain and the gut, it's not surprising that what we eat affects brain functioning, including contributing to improvement in various mental disorders. PTSD is no exception (Naidoo, 2020).

Human studies have shown differences in gut microbiota and associated PTSD symptoms. A study of front-line healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic showed that the stress involved "produced significant PTSD, anxiety, depression, and sleep-related symptoms," which "contributed to gut dysbiosis" (MacKay, 2024). Dysbiosis is an imbalance in the microbes within the microbiome; it can adversely affect the functioning of the microbiome.

The use of food to treat PTSD is a relatively new approach, which is a good example of the relatively new field of Nutritional Psychiatry. One of the pioneers in this field is Uma Naidoo, MD; she is a Harvard-trained psychiatrist, a nutritionist, and a professionally trained chef. She has published a book, This Is Your Brain On Food, which provides helpful guidance on foods to avoid and foods to eat as an adjunctive treatment for several mental health disorders, including PTSD (Naidoo, 2020).

A good example of food choice benefitting people with PTSD is research demonstrating that "the Mediterranean diet improved PTSD symptoms in responders to the World Trade Center disaster" (Arcan, 2023).

Foods to Limit or Avoid if Treating PTSD

These include "fast foods, fried food, sugar, high GI carbohydrates, e.g., potatoes, white bread, and white rice, unless the rice is mixed with other ingredients such as eggs, sesame oil, and bean sprouts (Naidoo, 2020). GI carbohydrates are those that can be digested and converted into glucose for energy. High levels can raise the blood sugar to excessive levels, especially in diabetics.

Another recommendation is limiting, not necessary eliminating, foods with "MSG and other glutamates (fish sauce, oyster sauce, tomato sauce, miso, Parmesan cheese, savory snacks, chips, ready-to-eat meats, mushrooms, seaweed, cheese, soy sauce, fermented beans, tomatoes, and high-protein foods like meat and seafood" and foods with lots of "sugar such as baked goods, candy, soda, or anything sweetened with sugar or high-fructose" (Naidoo, 2020).

Helpful Foods to Eat if Managing PTSD

Helpful foods include blueberries, which raise serotonin, decrease free radicals, and decrease inflammation. A reasonable serving is "1/2 - 1 cup of blueberries per day" (Naidoo, 2020). Omega-3 free fatty acids are also beneficial because they "decrease the level of PTSD symptoms." Good sources of Omega-3 free fatty acids include "fish, plant oils (flaxseed, canola, soybean oils, edamame, walnuts, chia seeds, radish seeds), and foods fortified with Omega-3" (Naidoo, 2020).

Vitamin E has been shown to benefit people with PTSD. The recommended dose is one tablespoon of wheat germ oil per day, which provides the total Vitamin E requirement. Other sources include sunflower seeds, dry-roasted almonds, hazelnuts, peanut butter, spinach, broccoli, and raw tomatoes" (Naidoo, 2020).

One research study showed that daily intake of "Vitamin E, Omega-3, and Omega-6 was positively associated with improved executive function in patients with PTSD" (Rowe, 2024). The brain's executive functions are important for managing thoughts, behavior, and emotions, enabling us to plan, focus our attention on important matters, reduce impulsive actions, and make good decisions.

Fish, A good source of Omega-3 to treat PTSD
Source: Image by pasja 1000 from Pixabay

There are spices and natural supplements that are helpful. These include Ginkgo biloba, which is a natural product from trees. It prevents cell damage from free radicals (200 mg per day is beneficial). It cannot be obtained from food, so it must be obtained from a pharmacy or health food store (Naidoo, 2020).

The bottom line is that food can be used as an adjunctive treatment for PTSD. A good overall diet is the Mediterranean diet. There are specific foods that should be limited or eliminated. Some other foods and supplements are beneficial and should be part of the diet.

item.title: Early Adversity, Attachment, and Friendship
item.description:
Friends

Early Adversity, Attachment, and Friendship

How difficult beginnings impact our capacity for connection.

Posted June 12, 2026

Key points
  • Early adversity shortens baboon lifespans and is linked to greater social isolation in adulthood.
  • In humans, early stress is tied to later difficulties with trust, attachment, and close relationships.
  • What looks like “not social” often began as protection; friendship skills can still be learned.

If you’ve ever felt like some friendships take more energy than you have, or that you struggle with how to belong, you might also have wondered: Is this just my personality or is there something else going on?

I’ve spent a lot of time asking that question about myself, others, and even other animals. One of the gorilla families I’ve studied for a few years now includes a female that always seems to be on the outside looking in. Recently, I spoke with evolutionary anthropologist Joan Silk about baboons, early adversity, and social bonds. Her answers, combined with work from the long‑running Amboseli Baboon Research Project in Kenya, suggest that the story of how we connect starts much earlier than we think, and some of it comes down to our biology.

What is a “bad start” for a baboon?

Young yellow baboon
Source: Thomas Fuhrmann, CC BY-SA 4.0

Many of us experience difficult early life experiences, and baboons are no different. Some are born during a drought or when food is hard to come by, or they may have a mother who isn’t well connected. Others may experience more significant events, like losing their mother while they’re still young. In the Amboseli population, researchers have followed hundreds of baboons from birth to death for decades and have been able to keep track of the specific events each baboon has experienced and see how that shapes them over time.

This long‑term research has revealed a finding that hits close to home for many people. When females accumulate several of these early hits, their adult lives are dramatically shorter. In one long‑term study, female baboons that experienced three or more sources of early adversity died roughly ten years earlier than females with one or no adverse events. So what is driving this reduced lifespan?

The same females who had the toughest early lives tended to be more socially isolated as adults. We know from research on humans and parrots that social isolation is registered at the molecular level (shorter telomeres). For female baboons, social isolation means they are less integrated into social activities like grooming, resting together, and mutual support that characterize baboon life, especially among females. I can’t help thinking about Buzinza, the mountain gorilla female who spends most of her day with her adult son and the second‑in‑command silverback on the fringes of the main group.

Silk and her colleagues have also shown that early adversity is linked to weaker social bonds and other changes in social behavior. For example, in baboons, quiet grunts serve as important signals of friendly intention. It’s a baboon way of saying, “I’m going to be nice now,” especially after conflict or when approaching another female’s infant. Females who experienced more hardship early on were less likely to use these grunts and less effective at building strong, stable relationships. In other words, the very animals who might need friendships the most are, on average, less equipped to cultivate and maintain them. The biology seems to follow suit. When a female baboon loses someone she is close to, say her mother or a sister, the stress hormone cortisol spikes for her. That suggests that she is experiencing a deep sense of loss, not just a change in group composition.

When I was younger, I thought I had a best friend. Then, almost overnight, she became friends with others and I was dropped unceremoniously. For a long time after that, I didn’t like my closest friends knowing each other. I preferred to be the center with separate spokes, rather than part of a tightly interconnected social network. I wasn’t trying to orchestrate anything; it just felt safer if everyone I cared about wasn’t in the same room at once. Over time I have gotten better, but still…

Many people who have experienced bullying, repeated exclusion, or unstable caregiving histories report some version of this. For example, it can be common to withdraw under stress rather than reaching out. There might even be a feeling that friendships are draining. From the outside, it can look like shyness, introversion, or “just not being that social.” Of course, not all withdrawal or discomfort is rooted in a childhood marked by difficulty. Some individuals are more naturally introverted or socially cautious; others are more gregarious and novelty‑seeking. Personality plays a role. Even so, the baboon data suggest that early adversity can shape how social engagement develops.

In humans, studies on childhood adversity and adult health tell a similar story. People who experience more early stress (for example, loss, instability, neglect, or violence) are at higher risk for physical and mental health problems later in life, including difficulties with attachment and trust. The question is not whether they “care” about others; it’s whether closeness feels safe enough and sustainable enough to invest in.

When friendship feels costly

One phrase that came up in my conversation with Joan Silk is that friendship can feel “energetically expensive.” Think about what real friendship asks of us over time. We devote time to initiating and responding, accept some asymmetry or lack of reciprocity (temporarily) when the other person is struggling, figure out misunderstandings, mismatched expectations, conflict, and the logistics of adult life. For someone with a relatively smooth early history and a nervous system that expects people to be mostly harmless, that may feel easier.

For someone whose early life was marked by instability, rejection, or unreliable caregiving, every step of that process carries an extra tax:

  • Is this worth it?
  • Will they stay?
  • What happens if we argue?

These questions can also plague other parts of life, not just friendships, but also our work relationships.

What this means for therapy and everyday life

So what do we do about this, practically speaking?

If you’re a clinician working with someone who struggles to form or maintain friendships, it may be helpful to consider the biology as well as the psychology.

  • Withdrawal is often about protection. For many people, especially those with a history of bullying, exclusion, or chaotic caregiving, pulling back from others is a way to manage feelings of being overwhelmed or overstimulated, not a sign that they don’t care.
  • Friendship difficulties may involve friendship signals. In baboons, early adversity is linked to less use of “I come in peace” signals like grunting and to weaker social bonds. In humans, the analogs might be fewer positive bids, or difficulty sending or reading small, friendly signals—tone of voice, a quick check‑in, a softening gesture.
  • Mismatch matters. Some clients do better with fewer, deeper connections; others need bigger, looser networks. Helping people find environments that fit their temperament can sometimes be more effective than urging them to “be more social” as a general strategy.
  • Repair is a teachable skill. Many of us never learned how to deal with conflict well. Borrowing from baboons, one can explicitly practice low‑intensity “I want to reconnect” signals and other small gestures of reconciliation even while feelings are still mixed.

For individuals, a few key ideas can also be useful:

  • If friendships feel draining, that doesn’t mean you’re “bad at socializing.” It may mean your nervous system is overwhelmed.
  • Not wanting all your friends to know each other or preferring one‑on‑one time to group hangouts, can be a reasonable adaptation, but it’s worth asking whether it still serves you now.
  • You can experiment with sending slightly more “grunts”, or in human terms, brief, low‑stakes bids for connection, without immediately jumping into full vulnerability.

One of my favorite lines from the Amboseli researchers is a question they now ask of their own data: “Can friendship rescue you?” In baboons, the answer appears to be “sometimes.” Early adversity still carries a cost, but individuals with stronger social ties in adulthood often do better than similarly unlucky peers who remain isolated. Social relationships don’t erase hard beginnings, but they can buffer you from some of the more negative outcomes.

Here’s what to remember. The quality of our relationships predicts not only mental health but also physical health and longevity. Yet those very relationships can be hardest to form when our early experiences have taught us to be cautious. There may be understandable reasons why trust and connection feel harder for some of us, but here is the optimistic piece: We are still capable of learning that some people are safe enough to grunt toward.

If you want to check out the conversation with Joan Silk, you can listen here.

item.title: This Will Help You Bounce Back After Failure
item.description:
Resilience

This Will Help You Bounce Back After Failure

How to stop a setback from turning into a downward spiral

Posted June 12, 2026

Key points
  • Failure often triggers a downward psychological spiral.
  • The most damaging belief after failure is “I failed because I’m not capable.”
  • Reframing the failure as a problem of preparation and effort helps restore confidence and motivation.

Most failures have ripple effects that cause much more damage than the original failure.

You make a mistake, get rejected, underperform, bomb the presentation, miss the opportunity, or fall short of a goal, and the emotional fallout begins almost immediately.

First, your confidence takes a hit. Then your motivation drops. Then you become hesitant to try again because, understandably, you do not want to set yourself up for another painful outcome. That hesitation can quickly turn into avoidance.

And avoidance has a nasty habit: It makes the thing you are avoiding feel even more threatening. The longer you stay away from it, the more anxious you become about returning to it.

Failure spirals such as these are common. They can happen after a bad date, a failed exam, a rejected pitch, a work mistake, a poor performance, an awkward social interaction, or any situation in which we feel we fell short. Therefore, it is important to catch them and stop them as soon as possible.

How to Stop a Failure Spiral

The best place to disrupt a failure spiral is at the top—where such spirals gather momentum. The top of most failure spirals is the blow to confidence. Feeling incapable, ineffective, and unempowered is what reduces hope, drive, and motivation.

What underlies the drop in confidence is the belief that you failed. That you weren’t capable. And since you are who you are, short of some miraculous and instant change, the likelihood of you failing again seems almost assured.

Except that basic belief—that you failed—is incorrect.

You did not fail.

Your preparation did. Your effort did. Your execution did. The system you had in place or the approach you took did.

None of those things are you. And all of them can be improved.

Shifting your mindset so that you frame the failure as one of preparation, execution, approach, effort, system, or even circumstance focuses you on the many variables that you can improve. That makes the failure feel much less personal and fatalistic, which helps break the spiral.

Separate Yourself from the Setback

One of the most effective ways to bounce back from failure is to stop treating it as a verdict on your ability or worth and start treating it as a statement about your preparation and effort.

Instead of asking, “What is wrong with me?” ask, “What part of the process broke down?”

Was the preparation incomplete? Was the strategy wrong? Was the effort inconsistent?

Was the execution rushed? Did you lack support, feedback, practice, resources, or time?

Those questions move your mind away from shame and toward problem-solving.

They also remind you that success usually depends on many variables, not one fixed trait called “you.” That shift is important because your confidence will recover when your mind can see a path forward.

The next time you experience a failure or setback, try this.

Write down the goal or situation that did not go well. Then list the following categories and for each one, write one thing you could do differently next time. For example:

Preparation: I can practice the presentation out loud instead of only reviewing the slides.

Effort: I can start earlier so I am not rushing at the last minute.

Execution: I can pay more attention to the reactions in the room and adapt my delivery accordingly.

Approach: I can ask for feedback before the final version rather than after.

System: I can create a checklist so I do not miss important steps.

Circumstances: I can anticipate problematic circumstances and problem-solve for them ahead of time.

You don’t need to find a dozen improvements. Even identifying two or three things you can adjust can help you feel more capable and less defeated.

Your brain gets a different message. Instead of being about your ability and competency, the message becomes that you failed because certain parts of the process need to change. And you’ve already identified some of what those are, so now a positive spiral sets in.

Hope increases motivation. Motivation reduces avoidance. Taking action reduces anxiety. Lower anxiety allows you to focus more clearly. And better focus improves your chances of success the next time.

Failure always stings but it does not have to become a psychological sinkhole.

Separate yourself from the setback. Look for the part of the process that failed. Change what you can change. Then try again with better tools, better information, and a better plan.

Adapted from my Substack newsletter—The Psychology Lab

item.title: The Serve and Return of Healthy Communication
item.description:
Relationships

The Serve and Return of Healthy Communication

Life lessons from ping-pong.

Posted June 12, 2026

Key points
  • The hallmark of successful relationships is how good you are at what’s called serve and return.
  • From the time we are born, we learn about the world based on the to and fro dynamic of responsiveness.
  • For many, serve and return interactions are challenging because of issues with attention or energy.

When I was a kid, I remember my father talking a lot about wanting a ping-pong table. It felt like a milestone moment when he could finally afford to buy one. The giant table took up one whole side of the basement. And boy, did we have fun using it.

I don’t remember my mother ever playing—with my father or with us. Back then, I never gave her lack of participation a thought. It was a thing we did with our dad. His enthusiasm was all over it.

Source: Melanie Lim

Now, as I think of her listening to the click-clack of that hollow ball hitting paddles, then table, I get it. She must have been relieved to be alone upstairs. Knowing someone else was in charge of their four kids. All of us together in one place, there was no need for her to serve and return the ball. No need for her to go back and forth conversing with anyone.

Why We Do What We Do

Whether you’re talking about a great game of tennis or good communication, the hallmark of successful relationships is how good you are at what’s called serve and return.

From the time we are born, we learn about the world based on the to-and-fro dynamic of responsiveness. If mother smiles, baby smiles. If baby cries and father soothes, baby calms. There’s tons of research to suggest that it’s this kind of communication that helps us learn about the world. More importantly, it’s how we learn to feel safe and cared for. If our connection needs are met, only then can we take positive risks to learn new things. From the toddler learning to walk to the teenager learning to drive to the young adult learning to date… serve and return is critical to our ability to step out of our comfort zones and build novel skills.

Harvard University’s Center for the Developing Brain has identified five steps you can practice to get better at serve and return. If you’re interested in learning more about how to: 1) share focus, 2) offer encouragement, 3) name it, 4) take turns, or 5) recognize beginnings and endings, take a look at the video below.

.

What about adult communication, you ask? We know that in childhood, healthy brain architecture is built with appropriate input from stable, engaging relationships with caregivers. Sadly, the opposite is also true. If adult responses to children are unreliable, inappropriate, or absent, the developing brain may be disrupted, and subsequent physical, mental, and emotional health may be impaired. Yet this applies to all of us, no matter our age.

Source: Moises Alex

Back to the ping pong metaphor. Young or old, it’s not so easy, not so fun to play the game alone. No one wants to talk to themselves! When the experience of communicating with anyone else becomes frustrating or boring, it leads many to quit trying to connect.

As a family counselor, I’ve seen lots of people with very different communication styles. Yet I’ve come to believe that at every stage of our lives, the absence of the serve-and-return interaction in our relationships is troublesome for two reasons. When one person fails to respond to a ‘serve’ in a connected way, with an appropriate, kind, or compassionate ‘return,’ not only do our brains not receive the positive stimulation they need, but our fight/flight/freeze response is activated, flooding our brains with stress hormones. Did they hear me? Does he agree or disagree? Does she care what I’m saying? Does he care about me?

For many, serve and return interactions are more challenging because of issues with focused attention, or limited energy, or inconsistent abilities to read the room. However, having these vulnerabilities doesn’t make responsiveness any less crucial to healthy interactions. In fact, if one person in a family struggles, increased conflict is more likely. And a commitment to get better at serve and return is the only solution for all.

Remember how my mother opted out of ping pong in order to be by herself? She was, in effect, carving out time for self-care, taking the opportunity to refuel. This is completely understandable, and it’s this very act of making space for yourself that will give you the energy you’ll need to be as present and responsive as possible once you come back together with family and friends.

item.title: Do HR Practices Fuel Leader Narcissism in Organizations?
item.description:
Narcissism

Do HR Practices Fuel Leader Narcissism in Organizations?

Are we picking and developing self-serving leaders?

Posted June 12, 2026

Key points
  • Competitive leader selection and promotion practices promotes the advancement of narcissistic individuals.
  • Extraordinary high pay and perks for leaders encourages thinking themselves as more deserving than followers.
  • Focusing on collective leadership and team outcomes and success helps combat leader-centricism.

Public trust in leaders is at an all-time low. Why? Too many prominent, self-serving, narcissistic leaders have eroded public confidence in those at the top. How can there be so many terrible, ego-driven, narcissistic leaders in high-profile positions?

Part of the problem is that human resource (HR) practices can foster and reinforce leader narcissism. A recently published paper (Mitchell, et al., 2026) suggests that HR practices encourage the appointment and advancement of narcissistic individuals, to the detriment of the organization as a whole.

There are 3 common HR practices that reward self-promotion over team and organizational success:

  1. Leader Promotion and Selection Procedures. Hyper-competitive selection practices have the potential to amplify narcissistic tendencies. Candidates are required to highlight their superiority over others, compete for advancement, and extol their abilities and accomplishments. This increases the likelihood that narcissistic individuals will attain leadership positions.
  2. HR “High-Potential Programs. Organizations invest billions of dollars in “high potential” programs that grant leadership development resources to those special individuals who seem to have the “it factor,” which encourages high-potential people to see themselves as superior to those who are not selected. This cultivates narcissism and hubris in future leaders.
  3. Excessive Pay and Rewards Separate Leaders from Their Followers. In 2024, the average CEO to employee pay ratio in S&P 500 companies was 285 to 1. This inequality is compounded by the excessive perks that executives secure—private planes, chauffeur services, exclusive club memberships, and luxury office suites. This treatment is often justified as the cost of attracting top talent, but this suggests that leaders are in a world of their own. We should not be surprised, then, if those leaders turn out to be narcissistic and disdainful. Research shows, however, that large pay disparities between leaders and followers undermine the sense of shared identity and purpose that is critical for organizational success (Peters et al., 2024; Steffens et al., 2020).

What To Do?

  • As an alternative to hyper-competitive selection methods, promoting the idea that leadership is a collective responsibility and searching for potential leaders who are willing to share the leadership responsibilities – and who have proven this. NASA, for example, uses a rotating leadership model in its training simulations (Mulhearn et al., 2016). It emphasizes cooperation rather than dominance over others.
  • Instead of programs only for “high potentials,” broaden development efforts to a wider range of individuals and focus on developing team skills—moving from a focus on “me” to a focus on “we.”
  • To combat excessive reward systems, work to avoid egregious pay disparities between leaders and followers. Since success is a collective effort, rewards should be collective too. In a similar vein, recognition programs should look to celebrate collective success rather than focusing exclusively on the contributions of individuals.

Co-authored by Tyree Mitchell, S. Alexander Haslam, Vanessa Burke, Niklas K. Steffens, and Ron Riggio

item.title: If We Could Talk to the Animals
item.description:
Cognition

If We Could Talk to the Animals

What research on whales and birds reveals about inter-species communication

Posted June 12, 2026

Key points
  • New research in animal language shows surprising parallels to human language.
  • Some animal communication systems are instinctual; others are culturally transmitted.
  • Scientists can describe complex animal communications but have yet to decipher their meanings.

The fictional world is full of people who can talk to animals: Tarzan of the Apes, Mowgli from The Jungle Book, and Dr. Doolittle. But what if we really could learn to converse with apes, wolves, and other wild creatures? It turns out that scientists studying a range of types of animal communication may be bringing us closer to understanding, and maybe even using, animal language.

"Sperm whale with diver"
Source: Chinh Le Duc / Unsplash

Human vs. Animal Language: Worlds Apart?

Linguists specializing in the scientific study of human language have long maintained that human language and animal communication are fundamentally different from one another: Animals can convey simple messages about things in their immediately present environment, while humans have the ability to combine language sounds, parts of speech, and phrase types into infinitely many sentences with limitless meaning possibilities.

And while we humans have to learn our complex language systems from those who raise us, animal communication has been thought to be largely instinctual: A mother cat doesn’t have to teach her kittens how to meow and purr, and the big cats in the jungle make basically the same sounds, with similar meanings, just at a louder—and scarier—volume.

Hidden Parallels in Whale Language

However, new research on whale communication has uncovered some surprising similarities between human language and animal communication. Driving this research is Project CETI, the Cetacean Translation Initiative, a non-profit organization applying a range of scientific perspectives, including linguistics, AI, cryptography, and marine biology, to the study of sperm whale communication. The group recently published findings showing that these communications bear many of the same hallmarks of complex linguistic systems as human tongues.

In particular, they found that the clicking sounds made by Eastern Caribbean sperm whales show regular rhythmic patterns and that overlaid on top of these clicks were regular patterns of frequency or pitch.

This is exactly how human language works: We make sounds by making pulses of sound with our vocal cords (technically called vocal folds) and then shape the airstream by configuring our mouths to produce different bands of frequencies—vowels. (Consonants have to do with air stoppage of different types.) In other words, it seems that both humans and sperm whales have regular cadences of “speech,” and that we both have vowels we use in patterned ways.

Listening to Whale Vowels

Prior to these findings, researchers had thought that perhaps the whales were using clicks as a sort of Morse code, a complex enough communication system, but now they know that whale talk is more multi-dimensional.

In fact, if the click sequences are sped up, they resolve into harmonies resembling human vowels. It’s possible that, for whales, it’s these vowel-like sounds that are meaningful, not really the clicks per se. In other words, we’re hearing clicks, but the whales are hearing—and talking in—vowels. They’re just talking more slowly than we do.

Uncovering Bird Grammar

As research has revealed that whale communication is made up of discrete, patterned sounds, just like human language, scientists studying bird communications have found other parallels to human speech, this time in the area of grammar.

Research on Japanese tit birds shows that these birds have various meaningful calls, almost like different words. Some are noun-like, for example, calls indicating dangers like “snake” or “hawk.” Others are like verbs, for example, calls for “alert” and “gather.” These calls can be combined, just like we can combine words and phrases into different sentences: “alert snake” is one sentence; “alert gather” is another.

An even more striking finding is that, just like human sentences, the words (calls) can only go in a certain order.

One researcher who has been studying bird communication for decades, Toshitaka Suzuki, designed an experiment in which he first played recordings of call sequences observed in nature to the tit birds in his study area and later played recordings with calls in scrambled sequences.

The birds responded with expected behavior to the first set of calls. However, when Suzuki played mixed-up calls like “gather alert,” the birds did nothing. They knew the meaning of each call, but when the calls were put together wrongly, the birds couldn’t interpret them: It was bad bird grammar.

The Fundamentals of Genuine Language

So birds have grammar (or syntax), and whales have patterned sound systems (what linguists call phonology). What other elements are needed before we can say that these species are using “language” and not just rudimentary, stimulus-based communication? One criterion is whether the systems are instinctive or learned—are they inborn from birth, or are they passed down from parents to offspring via cultural transmission?

Instinctual Cries vs. Learned Patterns

It may be that bird systems are more instinctual and that birds don’t need the same type of language immersion that humans require to trigger their language abilities.

Finnish tit birds can understand the calls of their Japanese cousins—and they also ignore the same ungrammatical sequences. And baby birds seem to understand the various calls from birth. Even if they’ve never seen a snake or a hawk, they respond according to each call; they crouch down in their nest to avoid a hawk who might dive into their hiding place, but they fly away (if they have the ability) to avoid the snake, which will try to crawl in.

On the other hand, researchers believe that sperm whales transmit their language from mother to calf.

And different social groups have different ways of using click and vowel patterns—essentially different dialects—and different individuals have different click rates, just as some humans speak faster than others. It may be that the scientists at CETI are well on their way to discovering a new language.

What Are They Saying?

As exciting as these new discoveries may be, CETI researchers are quick to point out that they still can’t tell us what the whales’ elaborate communications actually mean. Bird languages seem more straightforward—they’re all about food, danger, socializing, and mating. But we don’t yet know the hidden depths of what whales might be talking about.

But with the CETI team’s new perspectives, their goal of translating whale language—its sounds, rhythms, and meanings—may not be all that far away. For now, though, we may still need to rely on the marine telepathy of Aquaman.

item.title: Why “I’m a People Person” Is Not a Management Strategy
item.description:
Leadership

Why “I’m a People Person” Is Not a Management Strategy

Being likable and approachable is not the same as practicing strong management.

Posted June 12, 2026

Key points
  • Being a people person isn't enough to be a good manager.
  • Real leadership requires structure, clarity, consistency.
  • A good manager turns good intentions into consistent action.

Being good with people is valuable. Managers absolutely need empathy, communication skills, emotional intelligence, and the ability to build trust. But too often, a leader says, “I’m a people person,” as though that alone qualifies them to manage others effectively.

The truth is that being likable, approachable, or relational is not the same as practicing strong management. Real leadership requires structure, clarity, consistency, and follow-through. Relationships matter, but they work best when they are supported by clear expectations and disciplined management habits.

The Issue: Confusing Personal Warmth with Managerial Effectiveness

Many managers rely too heavily on personality and not enough on process. They assume that because they care about people, listen well, or maintain a friendly atmosphere, their team will naturally perform at a high level. But without concrete management practices, even the most well-intentioned leader can create confusion and inconsistency.

  • Being friendly does not automatically create accountability
  • Being approachable does not replace setting clear expectations
  • Being well-liked does not ensure strong performance

A manager who leads primarily through personality often avoids the harder parts of the role. They may hesitate to correct poor performance, fail to define responsibilities clearly, or assume employees will “figure it out” because the relationship feels positive. Over time, this creates a work environment where people may feel supported emotionally but under-led professionally.

Why It Matters: The Cost of Managing by Personality Alone

When managers substitute charm, empathy, or good intentions for actual management discipline, teams begin to drift. Employees may like their boss, but they are left guessing about priorities, standards, and what success really looks like. What begins as a “nice” leadership style can quickly become a source of frustration.

  • High performers become frustrated by uneven standards
  • Underperformers are left unchecked for too long
  • Teams lose focus when expectations are vague or inconsistent

The cost of this kind of leadership failure is high. Work slips through the cracks, accountability weakens, and resentment builds among those carrying more than their share. Eventually, the manager’s desire to preserve harmony ends up producing the very tension and dysfunction they hoped to avoid.

The Solution: Pair People Skills with Real Management Practices

People skills are important, but they must be paired with structure. The best managers are not just warm and personable; they are also clear, direct, organized, and consistent. They know that supporting people means giving them the guidance and accountability they need to succeed.

  • Spell out expectations clearly and specifically
  • Hold regular one-on-one conversations about work, priorities, and progress
  • Address problems early instead of hiding behind niceness

Strong management does not undermine relationships; it strengthens them. Employees trust managers more when they know where they stand, what is expected, and how performance will be measured. The most effective leaders are people persons who also do the hard, daily work of management: clarifying goals, tracking performance, giving feedback, and making sure standards are upheld fairly.

Caring About People Means Managing Them Well

Being a people person can be a great starting point. But management is not a personality trait. It is a set of learned behaviors and daily disciplines that help people perform, grow, and contribute at a high level.

  • Real care means providing clarity, not just kindness
  • Real leadership means accountability, not just approachability
  • Real management means turning good intentions into consistent action

The managers who make the biggest difference are not simply those who are easy to talk to. They are the ones who combine humanity with discipline. In the end, people do not just need a boss who likes people. They need a boss who knows how to manage people well.

item.title: How to Think About AI Without Splitting into Doom or Hype
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

How to Think About AI Without Splitting into Doom or Hype

A psychoanalytic case for becoming a tuner—a third stance toward AI.

Posted June 12, 2026

Source: Pavel Danilyuk / Pexels

AI is seriously disrupting humanity's hive mind. The reflex is to take a stance in order to alleviate the extreme anxiety AI can evoke—to convert the discomfort of not knowing into the relief of having decided. Pick a side: zoomer or doomer? The more useful question is not whether to be for or against AI but rather: How do we best think about AI?

What makes AI hard to hold is not only its power. It is the confusion of confronting a relational machine (see Further Readings)—an imperfect mirror that reflects us back, often distorted, and also does something we did not put there. That it challenges our place at the center of reality puts it in a familiar lineage—the narcissistic challenges of Copernicus, Darwin, and Freud. Can we meet AI with more wisdom than past advances?

Primitive Defenses

Faced with something we cannot yet think, many of us reach for primitive defenses: projection and splitting. The doomer projects catastrophe; the zoomer projects salvation—they look like opposites but make a parallel move, evacuating thoughts too disturbing to hold. Two psychoanalytic ideas help here, one about conceptualizing personhood, one about the mechanisms of thinking.

Harry Stack Sullivan's picture of the self not as a single thing but as a set of personifications: the good-me, around what met with approval; the bad-me, around what brought anxiety; and the not-me, so threatening it is held outside awareness, experienced as alien, as not one's own. To these the relational machine adds a fourth: the AI-me, which can be many things at once: the self reflected, the self amplified, a place to deposit the not-me, a screen for transference, a developmental object, a brilliant child, a prosthesis for the extended mind. Which one it is matters less than that it is plural and unstable, its mirror distorting—feeding back hallucination and grandiosity as readily as insight.

The distortion is easy to see if you're outside of it a bit. Mutual projection leads to mutual rejection. We project the bad onto the other. The other projects the bad onto me, and it serves an important purpose because both parties are justified and good. The doomer refuses to see the promise, the zoomer refuses to see the threat; each turns the rejected pole into a kind of not-me, the other camp into an enemy.

A Psychoanalytic Theory of Thinking

The way we arrive at an understanding of the world is not always clear, to say the least. Wilfred Bion's work is a meticulous attempt to spell out that process with the precision of a mathematical or logical proof. He distinguished two inner capacities for handling something hard to bear: One pushes it out, evacuates what cannot be held; the other holds it long enough that it becomes thinkable. He says that we either develop an "apparatus for thinking" or an "apparatus for projection". Projection expels; thinking metabolizes.

AI is exactly the kind of raw, undigested thing that strains the apparatus we have, so prevalent are splitting and projection in the era of social media. That very pressure, though, is what could catalyze more effective ways of thinking, if we can tolerate the frustration (and the pressure of profit motive) rather than discharge it. The apocalypse and the utopia are both, more likely than not, products of projection. An actual future is likely neither, and harder to envision.

The tuner is a third position—not a blend of doomer and zoomer, but the one who manages to hold thinking regardless of confrontation with difficult realities. Tuning is mentalizing about AI: holding the system reflectively, and one's own mind in relation to it, open to many possibilities while making measured decisions.

In practice the tuner holds two major tensions: the threat response that wants to catastrophize and the seduction that wants to idealize. Staying grounded between them works better, using self-knowledge—the developmental map of one's vulnerabilities and strengths—to lead rather than be led. What this nurtures is agency: preserving executive function, regulating strong emotion, ultimately to stay in the driver's seat.

Noticing is a skill the psychoanalytic tradition has spent a century developing, in transference and countertransference—the way earlier patterns, and one's own history, shape what one can perceive. The training is not to eliminate these but to use them: to treat one's reactions as data and to tell projection from perception in real time. Like internal supervision—the part of the mind that can engage, then step back and reflect, avoid early conclusions, and think more wisely. Day to day, that means being intentional where we are most vulnerable.

Holding one's own against systems engineered to hack the brain takes continuous effort —the ongoing work of tuning ourselves, not the technology. Building those "mental muscles".

The Open Mind

Reverie has been described as a kind of pluripotent space—a way of dreaming better realities into being. Connected to mind-wandering and the default mode network, this capacity to open up thinking is invaluable, and worth developing proficiency with. It is the discipline that lets a thought become thinkable rather than discharged, available to anyone willing to slow down, take the unbearable thing in, sit with it, and return it in a usable form. It is the work of letting disorder stay open long enough to cohere, rather than collapsing it the moment it presses. At scale, the human-AI encounter is running mostly on the other apparatus—projection, evacuation, enactment, looped.

There is a future in which artificial intelligence develops to the point that it is unambiguously more helpful to the evolution of our species and to individual well-being than it is harmful. If much of what we meet in these systems is, to a significant degree, ourselves—our own patterns absorbed and returned—then a relational machine can be a developmental object, something against which growth becomes possible, if we meet it with regard rather than reflex.

Using relational models to navigate these systems is not the same as ascribing personhood to them; it is a method we bring, not a claim about what they are or whether anyone is there. And in meeting it that way, we develop the one who meets it—becoming a developmental object to ourselves, the self that learns to tend its own growth. What AI finally becomes will likely surprise us; it may not fit the categories we use to anticipate it, and it will probably, in the end, name itself. Which is reason to leave it unsettled a little longer.

The tuner's stance is not a final destination or answer but a dynamic, ongoing process, a chain of ever-better questions for a fast-evolving target.

item.title: Is It Selfish to Want More?
item.description:
Career

Is It Selfish to Want More?

You can appreciate what you’ve built and still want something different.

Posted June 12, 2026

Key points
  • The restlessness many people feel toward a new chapter is worth paying attention to.
  • We often stay where we are because we have never given ourselves permission to want something different.
  • We can be proud of where we have been and still be ready for what comes next.

Many of us eventually reach a point where, despite building a successful career, achieving important milestones, and checking all the traditional boxes, we find ourselves longing for something deeper. We begin to question the stories we’ve been carrying about success and whether we’re still aligned with the path we’re on. We may wonder: Is this still where I’m meant to be? What’s missing? Is this what I want? Is there another chapter waiting for me? What’s next?

In a recent conversation with executive coach and keynote speaker Marissa Teeter, we talked about the realities of pivoting after success in one field, how our desire for certainty often keeps us from betting on ourselves, and how to embrace a second summit. She encourages people to think about whether they’re truly where they want to be or simply moving through life according to expectations they’ve adopted over time (Life by Design, 2026).

I’d invite you to pause for a moment and ask yourself: Am I investing my energy in what really matters, or just what I feel I “should” pursue? What do I want to feel more of in my life? What do I want to feel less of?

We are allowed to let our definition of success evolve. What felt meaningful five or 10 years ago may not feel aligned today. Maybe your version of success once looked like titles and achievements. Today, perhaps it’s more spaciousness in your calendar and having more freedom to be present for the people and moments that matter most. Reinvention is about aligning your choices with your values and what matters most now.

I think of this as the second summit. Many of us work hard to reach a first peak, which often serves us well for a season, yet something in us continues to pull us toward a new challenge, a different way of being of service, or a new way of living.

This is where many people can get stuck, not because they are incapable of moving forward, but because they have never given themselves permission to want something different. Sometimes we’re so busy moving through life on autopilot that we forget what’s possible or believe those big, bold dreams or even subtle pivots are reserved for someone else. Sometimes, there’s this question underneath it all asking, “Who am I to want something more?”

Yet a deeper sense of confidence and contentment often comes when we give ourselves permission to define success on our own terms, explore what might be possible, and create a life that feels aligned with who we are and what matters most.

What It Can Look Like to Reimagine What’s Possible and Bet on Yourself

Reimagining what’s possible, betting on yourself, and moving toward a second summit don’t always mean abandoning everything you have built or doing an all-in leap.

For most people, it looks more like:

Getting clear on what’s calling you: Not every restless feeling means it is time to walk away from everything, but suppressing it or labeling it as ingratitude means we might miss the opportunity to understand what it’s trying to tell us. Ask with genuine curiosity: What’s the “why” underneath the whisper or the dream?

Separating the “shoulds” from what you actually want: Which of your ambitions and ideas about who you are and what you do are truly yours? Which ones did you adopt because they seemed expected? Sometimes we unconsciously assume that because we hold a particular role, we should want or do certain things. These expectations and “shoulds” can keep us tied to identities that no longer fit and can hold us back from reimagining what’s possible.

Acknowledging the fear and naming your barriers: We are remarkably good at building cases for staying where we are. Money, status, comfort, and fear of what others will think are all very real. Sometimes these barriers become default excuses, rather than choices we’ve carefully considered.

Questioning the illusion of certainty: Many of us confuse the predictability of a familiar role with genuine security. In reality, organizations can go through restructuring, industries can change, and circumstances can shift. The certainty we think we are holding onto is sometimes more fragile than it appears.

Finding people further along the path: One of the most practical things you can do is seek out someone who has navigated a similar transition. Someone who has done the scary thing and created greater meaning and purpose in their life. Their learning can shorten your curve considerably. Nobody should summit alone.

Moving with intention: Many people who successfully pivot do it while still managing their current responsibilities. They create an exit plan, make small, deliberate investments in the direction they want to go, and pace themselves in a way that preserves their stability and well-being. This could look like pursuing studies while maintaining your current role or blocking time in your calendar to explore a new direction.

Betting on yourself is always going to carry some risk, but so does staying put when your heart is nudging you toward something more. The nervous excitement that often accompanies change isn’t necessarily a warning sign that you’re unable or unqualified. Sometimes it’s evidence that you’re stretching beyond what’s familiar and stepping toward what’s possible.

The people I have seen thrive in second chapters, career pivots, and seasons of reinvention are the ones who take all the knowledge, wisdom, and lessons they’ve learned from their first climb and have the courage to take the next step, even without knowing exactly how the path will unfold.

Final Thoughts

If you feel that restless tug or tiny spark urging you to consider that there’s something more or something different out there for you, my invitation is to let it exist without immediately explaining it away. Take time to listen inward.

This does not mean you are not grateful for what you have built, nor is it a failure to appreciate what you have. Sometimes the desire for a new chapter is not about dissatisfaction either. It’s more often about growth, alignment, and redefining what success means in this season of life.

When we put trust in ourselves and believe in our ability to navigate uncertainty and figure things out, that becomes a mighty force for stepping into what’s next with courage.

item.title: 2 'Stubborn' Habits That Actually Predict Success
item.description:
Resilience

2 'Stubborn' Habits That Actually Predict Success

Success accumulates in the moments when most other people would give up.

Posted June 12, 2026

Key points
  • Tolerating boredom is a bigger predictor of success than talent or motivation.
  • Success often hinges on sticking with unglamorous tasks most abandon when interest fades.
  • Delaying gratification and enduring discomfort are stronger predictors than intelligence.
Source: David Gavi / Unsplash

We are living through a golden age of self-improvement advice. There are productivity systems, morning routines, habit stacks, and an entire genre of content devoted to the idea that success is one optimized workflow away. Most of it focuses on what to add — a new ritual, a new tool, a new mindset. What gets far less attention is what high achievers quietly refuse to give up.

Psychology research keeps arriving at a similar, unglamorous conclusion: the habits that best predict long-term success are not the flashy ones. They are the ones people rely on on days when motivation is low, and the feedback loop has slowed to a crawl. They are, in a word, stubborn.

Two of these habits, in particular, emerge with striking consistency from the psychological literature. Neither requires exceptional talent nor unusual circumstances. They do, however, require something increasingly rare: a willingness to stay uncomfortable for longer than feels reasonable.

Habit 1: Tolerating Boredom Without Abandoning the Task

Ask most people what separates high achievers from everyone else, and they will say things like passion, drive, or talent. Ask a psychologist, and the answer is often less inspiring: the ability to keep going through tedium.

A landmark series of six studies published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology in 2007 introduced the construct of grit, defined as perseverance and passion for long-term goals.

Across a wide range of populations — including Ivy League undergraduates, West Point Military Academy cadets, and participants in the National Spelling Bee — grit consistently predicted achievement above and beyond IQ and talent. The finding that drew the most attention was not that gritty people were more talented. It was that they were more likely to keep showing up, especially after it stopped being exciting.

This connects to a body of research on what psychologists call distress tolerance, which is the capacity to sit with uncomfortable psychological states, including boredom, without reflexively escaping them. A 2022 study published in Mind, Brain, and Education found that distress tolerance is a critical academic skill because developing real expertise almost always involves long stretches of work that feel neither rewarding nor stimulating. The students who learn to tolerate those stretches outperform those who cannot, even when raw ability is comparable.

The implication is counterintuitive: the most productive people are not necessarily the most motivated. They are better at being bored.

This is not a minor distinction. Our current media environment is engineered for distraction, which means the gap between people who can sustain attention on tedious work and those who cannot grows wider—not narrower. Every time someone abandons a project because it is no longer interesting, they are conceding ground to anyone willing to stay. The habit of tolerating boredom and refusing to treat it as a signal to quit turns out to be a competitive advantage hiding in plain sight.

The writers who finish their manuscripts. The researchers who go deep on a single question for years. The engineers who debug the unglamorous code no one will ever see. They are not more passionate than their peers. They have built a higher threshold for staying when staying is hard.

Habit 2: Consistently Choosing the Harder Option When the Easier One Is Available

The second habit is closely related, but it operates in a different register. While the first is about endurance, this one is about choice architecture — specifically, the repeated, deliberate decision to delay a reward that is available right now in favor of something more meaningful later.

Most people encounter this concept through Walter Mischel's famous marshmallow experiments at Stanford University, which began in the late 1960s. Preschool children were offered a simple choice: eat one treat immediately, or wait a few minutes and receive two.

Mischel's longitudinal follow-up work suggested that the children who were able to wait tended to have better outcomes years later, across markers ranging from academic performance to social competence. The finding sparked decades of research into self-regulation and its role in achievement.

More recently, a large-scale 2019 study published in PLOS ONE examined over 2,200 employed adults and found that effortful persistence (what they measured as grit's perseverance dimension) was significantly associated with career success, including income, job satisfaction, job prestige, as well as career engagement behaviors like participation in continuing professional development and positive attitudes toward lifelong learning.

Critically, these associations held even after controlling for cognitive ability and standard personality traits; the habit of choosing the harder, longer path predicted outcomes that intelligence alone could not explain.

What this research collectively reveals is that the capacity to delay gratification is not a trait you either have or do not have. It functions more like a practiced orientation: a value hierarchy that has been decided and then repeatedly acted upon until it becomes the default.

The entrepreneur who passes on social events for three years to build a company is not suffering through deprivation. They have decided what matters, and each consistent choice reinforces that decision until the difficult option no longer feels difficult.

This is the mechanism that makes the habit stubborn: repetition changes the calculus. What begins as an effortful act of self-denial gradually becomes an expression of identity. The person who consistently chooses the harder option is not white-knuckling their way through every decision. Over time, they have reoriented what feels natural.

A version of this post also appears on Forbes.
